task.description:
Implement a simple dev script for local Codex plugin install, uninstall, and update.
User's full request: 'work with claude to implement a dev script for this operation. it should be able to install, uninstall, or update gracefully. you review and push back'
Context: Earlier we gave commands npm run build, npm run release:assemble, codex plugin remove subagent-extension-for-codex@demo-user, codex plugin marketplace remove demo-user, codex plugin marketplace add ./release, codex plugin add subagent-extension-for-codex@demo-user. The goal is one repo dev entrypoint with install/uninstall/update operations. Read AGENTS.md and required relevant docs/code first. Keep it simple. Do not commit. Add concise dev docs and meaningful focused tests following existing patterns. Investigate actual Codex CLI idempotency and same-version local rebuild behavior in a temporary isolated CODEX_HOME before relying on assumptions. Never change user's real Codex installation or stop their service during validation. Uninstall must be graceful if absent, genuine errors must not be swallowed, builds must succeed before removing existing installation, preserve task data. Consider transition from remote marketplace sharing the name, and explain any limits. Avoid service lifecycle scope creep. Send me your proposed approach after inspection then implement. I will review and request corrections.
context: Working tree initially clean. Use existing project workflow and canonical local release assembled by scripts/assemble-release.mjs. Codex CLI marketplace upgrade only refreshes Git marketplaces. Earlier tiny probe found local marketplace add repeated is idempotent, but plugin add behavior not established (probe manifest layout was wrong).

instructions.message: Review concern to address: docs/task-continuation.md says same-version service with installRoot still present is reused. Reinstalling a same-version local build into the same cache path may leave old running backend code even after restarting Codex. Keep service control out of scope, but docs/output must explicitly explain any needed manual service restart and impact on running turns. Do not claim restarting Codex alone activates backend rebuilds if probe/code doesn't establish that. Also prefer querying installed state over broad || true error swallowing.

Approach looks suitably small. Pushback: keep --no-build only if it has a clear developer use too (e.g. frontend iteration already built); document that it still assembles current dist. Add meaningful build-failure preservation and genuine CLI failure propagation coverage rather than only happy path sequencing. You can use temporary miniature checkout/build scripts and/or fake executables following existing development integration suites to avoid full builds for those failures. Retain real CLI coverage for same-version overwrite/stale-file removal, twice uninstall, source switch. Do not add parser-only unit tests. Verify how plugin list behaves for orphaned config after marketplace removal, so uninstall doesn't falsely skip an installed entry if discovery omits it. No auto restoring remote sources needed.

Review of current script: isLocalRelease calls realpathSync(entry.marketplaceSource.source) without checking that source still exists. A deleted old checkout/release can make uninstall/update throw before cleanup. Handle that ordinary stale-path case and cover it. Reject extra/unknown args before building instead of silently treating e.g. 'uninstall --typo' as valid. Also confirm CLI invocation on Windows: existing marketplace integration resolves npm codex.cmd to its JS entrypoint. Reuse a minimal appropriate approach or clearly bound supported script platforms, without large helper abstraction. I see --no-build currently omitted, fine if miniature build fixtures make it unnecessary.

If stale source makes marketplace list unusable, reconsider simpler unconditional plugin remove then targeted marketplace remove, handling ONLY the probed exact absent-marketplace error as no-op (with a concise comment) instead of querying state or parsing Codex config internals. Then add local marketplace+plugin for install/update. That resets source every time, but removes branching/path probes and supports orphaned state. Genuine remove/list failures must surface. Use your judgment from probe, but avoid growing machinery just to preserve redundant marketplace registration.

Please don't add TOML parsing/config internals for this. Follow simpler unconditional targeted removals suggested in my last steer. Graceful absent-marketplace handling may rely on exact known diagnostic, fail closed on anything else and test that distinction. It is appropriate for this dev wrapper, easier to maintain than mirroring Codex config ownership.

Final review notes as you finish: absent error uses stderr.includes(), which can hide an additional real error alongside that phrase. Prefer matching the complete known error diagnostic (and expected exit status 1) so unknown output fails closed, with a failure case guarding near-match/additional errors. Ensure tests now remove stale /Replacing marketplace/ assertion. Docs should explicitly bound macOS/Linux if keeping Windows shim support out of scope. Keep current concise implementation, no further abstractions needed.

I ran actual npm run dev:plugin install with temp CODEX_HOME. Full build passed, assembly hit sandbox EPERM on default ~/.npm cache. Rerunning with temporary npm_config_cache, no code change needed. Please finish your formatting/checks and report, I'll independently verify final diff.

User approved follow-up: 'should we prompt the user for a service kill or restart if needed?' We proposed optional default-No prompt for plugin-owned running service after install/update ('Stop the running service so the new build can load? This interrupts active turns. [y/N]') and after uninstall ('Also stop the running service? This interrupts active turns. [y/N]'). Skip prompts in noninteractive runs unless explicit --stop-service. SIGTERM only after verifying process ownership. Existing launcher starts new service on next connection, don't spawn daemon yourself. User says 'let’s do it'. Implement this follow-up, no commit, keep it simple, read relevant existing lifecycle docs/code first. Existing script/tests/docs are uncommitted baseline from your last turn, retain them. Reuse process identity/ownership helpers if suitable (src/service/platform/service/process-info.ts has inspectProcessIdentity, inspectProcess, isExtensionService, isSameProcess; serve.ts writes service.json identity/launcher/installRoot). Must refuse PID-reused, foreground/dev-owned, mismatched metadata or ownership. Honor SUBAGENT_EXTENSION_FOR_CODEX_DATA and default path. Recheck after waiting at prompt before sending SIGTERM. No SIGKILL. Default leaves service running. Show actionable result for stopped/already gone/refused. Use isolated fake services and temporary data only for tests, NEVER stop real user's service or the live service running this Claude task. Test actual stop, no flag noninteractive leave running, identity mismatch/foreground refusal, prompt default no/accept as practical via PTY or focused helper tests. Build failures must never prompt/stop. Docs update canonical local build section. Send proposed approach after inspection then implement. I'll review ownership and race handling and push back.

Good pushback: use existing authenticated drain API, approved. This better fits graceful update and avoids duplicating process ownership. Explain limits accurately: turns finish up to 10 minutes, then interrupted; don't claim never interrupted. Reuse challenge proof, require launcher stdio, finite fetch timeouts, strict loopback origin, redirect:'error' for proof/drain (never send credentials to redirected targets). No direct PID signaling fallback. Node24 supports type stripping for health-proof.ts if self-contained, so avoid tsx npm entry change if plain node suffices, and ensure miniature checkout fixtures copy required module/import dependencies. Fake HTTP tests need sandbox localhost listeners allowed: our shell sandbox likely denies, so request escalation up front for tests requiring listeners if needed per AGENTS. Keep helper feature-owned and implementation modest. No need automatically detect active backend differences, prompt for running plugin-owned service is fine.

Confirmed parent shell sandbox denies loopback bind (EPERM). I'm obtaining escalation for isolated HTTP verification. Your worker may have different sandbox, but don't skip HTTP tests on bind denial. Let me run your final suites escalated if your environment cannot bind.

Please make requested-stop failures distinguishable: if user accepts prompt or passes --stop-service and auth/ownership/drain verification fails, report operation installed/uninstalled but stop failed and return nonzero. Missing/already exited is success, default no or noninteractive skip is success. Never expose tokens in fetch errors/logs. Keep status/output scope honest: drain requested, not already stopped/restarted. Automatic restart after uninstall isn't promised (old connected proxies can still exist).

Review current service flow: (1) Require drain response HTTP 202 and JSON status:'draining' (handle malformed body) before reporting requested stop success. (2) Avoid echoing invalid service.json URL with credentials in error output. (3) After prompt re-probe should not blindly stop a different plugin service that replaced the offered one meanwhile. Return stable candidate metadata identity from service.json (pid/startedAt/origin) and compare after prompt, or equivalent small check; refuse changed candidate so we don't drain the new just-started build. Add focused test service changes while prompt waits. (4) service logic is ~230 lines added to 94-line CLI. Consider separate scripts/dev-plugin-service.mjs owning discovery/auth/prompt/drain with one exported function; CLI owns operation sequencing. Keep narrow and avoid configurable test-only abstraction.

Helper review looks good. Small final consistency fix: plain-loopback origin validation should reject pathname other than '/', search, hash too, matching launcher.ts loopbackUrl. Current validation silently strips these via url.origin. Ensure health identity metadata in test fixtures includes pid/startedAt so replacement test models actual service.json. I verified escalated loopback bind succeeds and can run final suites when ready.

I reviewed helper and tests and am independently running your 12 tests plus existing service-drain-http suite with escalation for loopback. Please finish docs/format/lint/Knip/test TypeScript checks, no need repeat passed behavior tests unless you change code. Report final reply when done.

// Assembles the built package as a Codex marketplace that is also the plugin,
// the package the release publishes to npm. Run after `npm run build`:
//   node scripts/assemble-release.mjs [--out release]
import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
import {
  cpSync,
  existsSync,
  mkdirSync,
  readFileSync,
  rmSync,
  writeFileSync,
} from "node:fs";
import { dirname, join, resolve } from "node:path";
import { parseArgs } from "node:util";

/**
 * main's marketplace. Its name becomes the plugin ID's suffix
 * (subagent-extension-for-codex@demo-user) and part of Codex's PLUGIN_DATA
 * path, so it must never change. The release reuses it, so an install from the
 * release keeps the same ID and data.
 */
const marketplace = JSON.parse(
  readFileSync(".agents/plugins/marketplace.json", "utf8"),
);

const { values } = parseArgs({
  options: { out: { type: "string", default: "release" } },
});

const out = resolve(values.out);

for (const entry of ["dist/main.js", "dist/stdio.js", "dist/app.html"]) {
  if (!existsSync(entry)) {
    throw new Error(`${entry} is missing; run npm run build first`);
  }
}

// Under npm, its own script runs through this Node, since Windows can't start
// the npm.cmd shim without a shell. tests/support/npm.ts does the same.
const npmCli = process.env.npm_execpath;
const npm = npmCli?.endsWith(".js") ? [process.execPath, npmCli] : ["npm"];

// npm's file list, so the plugin and any npm package ship the same files.
const [{ files }] = JSON.parse(
  execFileSync(
    npm[0],
    [...npm.slice(1), "pack", "--dry-run", "--json", "--ignore-scripts"],
    { encoding: "utf8", maxBuffer: 64 * 1024 * 1024 },
  ),
);

rmSync(out, { recursive: true, force: true });

for (const { path } of files) {
  mkdirSync(dirname(join(out, path)), { recursive: true });
  cpSync(path, join(out, path));
}

// Nothing installs dependencies or runs scripts from the release. The
// manifest only marks the package root and carries its metadata.
const manifest = JSON.parse(readFileSync("package.json", "utf8"));

const slim = Object.fromEntries(
  [
    "name",
    "version",
    "description",
    "license",
    "author",
    "homepage",
    "repository",
    "bugs",
    "type",
    "engines",
  ]
    .filter((key) => key in manifest)
    .map((key) => [key, manifest[key]]),
);

writeFileSync(join(out, "package.json"), `${JSON.stringify(slim, null, 2)}\n`);

mkdirSync(join(out, ".agents/plugins"), { recursive: true });

writeFileSync(
  join(out, ".agents/plugins/marketplace.json"),
  `${JSON.stringify(
    {
      name: marketplace.name,
      interface: marketplace.interface,
      plugins: [
        {
          name: manifest.name,
          source: { source: "local", path: "./" },
          category: "Coding",
        },
      ],
    },
    null,
    2,
  )}\n`,
);

console.log(
  `Release ${manifest.version}: ${files.length} files in ${out}; install as ${manifest.name}@${marketplace.name}`,
);

// Assembles the built package as a Codex marketplace that is also the plugin,
// the package the release publishes to npm. Run after `npm run build`:
//   node scripts/assemble-release.mjs [--out release]
import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
import {
  cpSync,
  existsSync,
  mkdirSync,
  readFileSync,
  rmSync,
  writeFileSync,
} from "node:fs";
import { dirname, join, resolve } from "node:path";
import { parseArgs } from "node:util";

/**
 * main's marketplace. Its name becomes the plugin ID's suffix
 * (subagent-extension-for-codex@demo-user) and part of Codex's PLUGIN_DATA
 * path, so it must never change. The release reuses it, so an install from the
 * release keeps the same ID and data.
 */
const marketplace = JSON.parse(
  readFileSync(".agents/plugins/marketplace.json", "utf8"),
);

const { values } = parseArgs({
  options: { out: { type: "string", default: "release" } },
});

const out = resolve(values.out);

for (const entry of ["dist/main.js", "dist/stdio.js", "dist/app.html"]) {
  if (!existsSync(entry)) {
    throw new Error(`${entry} is missing; run npm run build first`);
  }
}

// Under npm, its own script runs through this Node, since Windows can't start
// the npm.cmd shim without a shell. tests/support/npm.ts does the same.
const npmCli = process.env.npm_execpath;
const npm = npmCli?.endsWith(".js") ? [process.execPath, npmCli] : ["npm"];

// npm's file list, so the plugin and any npm package ship the same files.
const [{ files }] = JSON.parse(
  execFileSync(
    npm[0],
    [...npm.slice(1), "pack", "--dry-run", "--json", "--ignore-scripts"],
    { encoding: "utf8", maxBuffer: 64 * 1024 * 1024 },
  ),
);

rmSync(out, { recursive: true, force: true });

for (const { path } of files) {
  mkdirSync(dirname(join(out, path)), { recursive: true });
  cpSync(path, join(out, path));
}

// Nothing installs dependencies or runs scripts from the release. The
// manifest only marks the package root and carries its metadata.
const manifest = JSON.parse(readFileSync("package.json", "utf8"));

const slim = Object.fromEntries(
  [
    "name",
    "version",
    "description",
    "license",
    "author",
    "homepage",
    "repository",
    "bugs",
    "type",
    "engines",
  ]
    .filter((key) => key in manifest)
    .map((key) => [key, manifest[key]]),
);

writeFileSync(join(out, "package.json"), `${JSON.stringify(slim, null, 2)}\n`);

mkdirSync(join(out, ".agents/plugins"), { recursive: true });

writeFileSync(
  join(out, ".agents/plugins/marketplace.json"),
  `${JSON.stringify(
    {
      name: marketplace.name,
      interface: marketplace.interface,
      plugins: [
        {
          name: manifest.name,
          source: { source: "local", path: "./" },
          category: "Coding",
        },
      ],
    },
    null,
    2,
  )}\n`,
);

console.log(
  `Release ${manifest.version}: ${files.length} files in ${out}; install as ${manifest.name}@${marketplace.name}`,
);

data.content:
UI needs no restart. If the file disappears, as when a plugin update removes the
running installation before handover, the service serves the last copy it read.

## Build

`npm run build` regenerates validation schemas, cleans `dist/`, type checks the
service, and builds the service entrypoints and `dist/app.html`. Each build
rejects imports from the other runtime, development tooling and tests.

- The service bundle includes its runtime packages, so an extracted package runs
  without `node_modules`. It ships no Claude Code binary and launches the
  installed [Claude Code CLI](claude-cli.md).
- Bundling drops package license files, so each build collects them into
  `dist/THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt` for the service and
  `dist/app.html.THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt` for the panel.
- Source maps omit embedded sources and map stack traces to the original files.
- Bundles live in `dist/bundle/`. The public entries `dist/main.js`,
  `dist/stdio.js` and `dist/projects-cli.js` are small ES2017 guards. Each
  checks Node against `engines.node`, prints what to install on an old runtime,
  then imports its bundle.

`npm run package:plugin` builds and packs the plugin. The package holds only
what the installed plugin runs or shows: `dist/`, `migrations/`, `assets/`,
`skills/`, `plugin.json`, `mcp.json`, the README and `LICENSE`. Guides stay on
GitHub, so the README's links to `docs/` don't resolve inside an extracted
package.

`npm run release:assemble`, run after a build, writes `release/`, the package
the release publishes to npm. It holds the packed files, a manifest with no
scripts or dependencies, and an `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` that lists
the plugin with source `./`. The directory is both a Codex marketplace and the
plugin. Install it locally with:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add ./release
codex plugin add subagent-extension-for-codex@demo-user
```

Adding the checkout itself (`codex plugin marketplace add ./`) adds `main`'s
marketplace, which installs the version it lists from npm, so test local builds
with `./release`.

The assembled marketplace takes its name and display name from `main`'s. The
name `demo-user` is part of the plugin ID and its `PLUGIN_DATA` path, so it
must not change.

Two package suites in `npm test` cover the result:

- `tests/integration/package/packed-artifact.test.ts` checks startup,
  transports, CLI readiness and restarts from an extracted package outside the
  checkout. It fails if the package's top-level file list changes.
- `tests/integration/package/marketplace-install.test.ts` assembles a release
  from `dist/`, packs it with npm and installs the extracted package with the
  Codex CLI into a temporary `CODEX_HOME`. It runs the MCP command Codex reports
  against an isolated data directory and port. It checks the reported version,
  tool listing and calls, and service startup. It needs the Codex CLI
  (`CODEX_BIN` or `codex` on `PATH`) and skips without it.

To run the marketplace test alone after a build:

```sh
npx vitest run tests/integration/package/marketplace-install.test.ts
```

Set `MARKETPLACE_SOURCE` to a published marketplace, such as
`owner/repo@v1.2.3`, to install that instead. Its version must match the
checkout's `package.json`. The release workflow does this after publishing.

## Releasing

Users add `main`'s marketplace, `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json`, which
Codex adds and builds Claude's events with the fixture `Timeline`. A step's
`reply` holds the message that ends Claude's turn, which playback streams.
Playback timing lives in `dev/panel/showcase/playback.ts`. The Codex look lives
in `dev/panel/showcase/codex/`. Update it there when Codex changes.

The showcase loads `dev/panel/host/panel.html?now=<ms>`, which freezes the
panel's clock, so elapsed times are the same in every capture. During playback
`&tick` lets the clock run, and the showcase moves it forward as events arrive.

## Connect Codex from a checkout

Installed users get the plugin from the marketplace
([README](../README.md#install)). To run a checkout instead, build it, pick one
transport and add its example to `~/.codex/config.toml`. Both transports expose
the same task tools and MCP App.

- Remove the plugin first, or Codex runs both servers.
- Replace the existing server entry when switching transports. Do not combine
  stdio and HTTP settings.
- To return to the plugin, delete `[mcp_servers.subagent_extension_for_codex]` and
  its `env` or `http_headers` tables, and stop the checkout's service. The
  plugin never stops a service it didn't start.

See the
[Codex MCP configuration reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp#configure-with-configtoml)
for supported options.

// Opens the release pull request from an up-to-date main:
//   npm run release:prepare [-- <version>]
// Without a version, it picks the next one from the conventional commits since
// the last release and asks to confirm it. Without a CHANGELOG.md section for
// the version, it drafts one from the feat and fix commits. The pull request
// starts as a draft while the notes are reviewed. See
// docs/development.md#releasing.
import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { createInterface } from "node:readline/promises";

const run = (command, args) =>
  execFileSync(command, args, { encoding: "utf8" }).trim();

function fail(message) {
  console.error(message);
  process.exit(1);
}

if (run("git", ["branch", "--show-current"]) !== "main") {
  fail("Run this on main");
}

run("git", ["fetch", "--quiet", "--tags", "origin", "main"]);

if (
  run("git", ["rev-parse", "HEAD"]) !== run("git", ["rev-parse", "origin/main"])
) {
  fail("main must match origin/main");
}

const changed = execFileSync("git", ["status", "--porcelain"], {
  encoding: "utf8",
})
  .split("\n")
  .filter(Boolean)
  .map((line) => line.slice(3));

// The last release on main. Unmerged prerelease tags aren't on main.
const [since] = run("git", [
  "tag",
  "--merged",
  "HEAD",
  "--list",
  "v*",
  "--sort=-v:refname",
]).split("\n");

const messages = run("git", [
  "log",
  "--format=%B%x00",
  since ? `${since}..HEAD` : "HEAD",
])
  .split("\0")
  .map((message) => message.trim())
  .filter(Boolean);

const subjects = messages.map((message) => message.split("\n")[0]);

/** The next version after the last release, by semver from the commit types. */
function nextVersion() {
  if (!since) fail("There's no release tag yet, so pass a version");

  const [major, minor, patch] = since.slice(1).split(".").map(Number);

  const breaking = messages.some(
    (message) =>
      /^\w+(\(.+?\))?!:/.test(message) || /^BREAKING CHANGE:/m.test(message),
  );

  // Before 1.0, a breaking change bumps the minor version.
  if (breaking && major > 0) return `${major + 1}.0.0`;

  if (
    breaking ||
    subjects.some((subject) => /^feat(\(.+?\))?:/.test(subject))
  ) {
    return `${major}.${minor + 1}.0`;
  }

rejects imports from the other runtime, development tooling and tests.

- The service bundle includes its runtime packages, so an extracted package runs
  without `node_modules`. It ships no Claude Code binary and launches the
  installed [Claude Code CLI](claude-cli.md).
- Bundling drops package license files, so each build collects them into
  `dist/THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt` for the service and
  `dist/app.html.THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt` for the panel.
- Source maps omit embedded sources and map stack traces to the original files.
- Bundles live in `dist/bundle/`. The public entries `dist/main.js`,
  `dist/stdio.js` and `dist/projects-cli.js` are small ES2017 guards. Each
  checks Node against `engines.node`, prints what to install on an old runtime,
  then imports its bundle.

`npm run package:plugin` builds and packs the plugin. The package holds only
what the installed plugin runs or shows: `dist/`, `migrations/`, `assets/`,
`skills/`, `plugin.json`, `mcp.json`, the README and `LICENSE`. Guides stay on
GitHub, so the README's links to `docs/` don't resolve inside an extracted
package.

`npm run release:assemble`, run after a build, writes `release/`, the package
the release publishes to npm. It holds the packed files, a manifest with no
scripts or dependencies, and an `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` that lists
the plugin with source `./`. The directory is both a Codex marketplace and the
plugin. Install it locally with:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add ./release
codex plugin add subagent-extension-for-codex@demo-user
```

Adding the checkout itself (`codex plugin marketplace add ./`) adds `main`'s
marketplace, which installs the version it lists from npm, so test local builds
with `./release`.

The assembled marketplace takes its name and display name from `main`'s. The
name `demo-user` is part of the plugin ID and its `PLUGIN_DATA` path, so it
must not change.

Two package suites in `npm test` cover the result:

- `tests/integration/package/packed-artifact.test.ts` checks startup,
  transports, CLI readiness and restarts from an extracted package outside the
  checkout. It fails if the package's top-level file list changes.
- `tests/integration/package/marketplace-install.test.ts` assembles a release
  from `dist/`, packs it with npm and installs the extracted package with the
  Codex CLI into a temporary `CODEX_HOME`. It runs the MCP command Codex reports
  against an isolated data directory and port. It checks the reported version,
  tool listing and calls, and service startup. It needs the Codex CLI
  (`CODEX_BIN` or `codex` on `PATH`) and skips without it.

To run the marketplace test alone after a build:

```sh
npx vitest run tests/integration/package/marketplace-install.test.ts
```

Set `MARKETPLACE_SOURCE` to a published marketplace, such as
`owner/repo@v1.2.3`, to install that instead. Its version must match the
checkout's `package.json`. The release workflow does this after publishing.

## Releasing

Users add `main`'s marketplace, `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json`, which
Codex adds and builds Claude's events with the fixture `Timeline`. A step's
`reply` holds the message that ends Claude's turn, which playback streams.
Playback timing lives in `dev/panel/showcase/playback.ts`. The Codex look lives
in `dev/panel/showcase/codex/`. Update it there when Codex changes.

The showcase loads `dev/panel/host/panel.html?now=<ms>`, which freezes the
panel's clock, so elapsed times are the same in every capture. During playback
`&tick` lets the clock run, and the showcase moves it forward as events arrive.

## Connect Codex from a checkout

Installed users get the plugin from the marketplace
([README](../README.md#install)). To run a checkout instead, build it, pick one
transport and add its example to `~/.codex/config.toml`. Both transports expose
the same task tools and MCP App.

- Remove the plugin first, or Codex runs both servers.
- Replace the existing server entry when switching transports. Do not combine
  stdio and HTTP settings.
- To return to the plugin, delete `[mcp_servers.subagent_extension_for_codex]` and
  its `env` or `http_headers` tables, and stop the checkout's service. The
  plugin never stops a service it didn't start.

See the
[Codex MCP configuration reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp#configure-with-configtoml)
for supported options.

// Opens the release pull request from an up-to-date main:
//   npm run release:prepare [-- <version>]
// Without a version, it picks the next one from the conventional commits since
// the last release and asks to confirm it. Without a CHANGELOG.md section for
// the version, it drafts one from the feat and fix commits. The pull request
// starts as a draft while the notes are reviewed. See
// docs/development.md#releasing.
import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { createInterface } from "node:readline/promises";

const run = (command, args) =>
  execFileSync(command, args, { encoding: "utf8" }).trim();

function fail(message) {
  console.error(message);
  process.exit(1);
}

if (run("git", ["branch", "--show-current"]) !== "main") {
  fail("Run this on main");
}

run("git", ["fetch", "--quiet", "--tags", "origin", "main"]);

if (
  run("git", ["rev-parse", "HEAD"]) !== run("git", ["rev-parse", "origin/main"])
) {
  fail("main must match origin/main");
}

const changed = execFileSync("git", ["status", "--porcelain"], {
  encoding: "utf8",
})
  .split("\n")
  .filter(Boolean)
  .map((line) => line.slice(3));

// The last release on main. Unmerged prerelease tags aren't on main.
const [since] = run("git", [
  "tag",
  "--merged",
  "HEAD",
  "--list",
  "v*",
  "--sort=-v:refname",
]).split("\n");

const messages = run("git", [
  "log",
  "--format=%B%x00",
  since ? `${since}..HEAD` : "HEAD",
])
  .split("\0")
  .map((message) => message.trim())
  .filter(Boolean);

const subjects = messages.map((message) => message.split("\n")[0]);

/** The next version after the last release, by semver from the commit types. */
function nextVersion() {
  if (!since) fail("There's no release tag yet, so pass a version");

  const [major, minor, patch] = since.slice(1).split(".").map(Number);

  const breaking = messages.some(
    (message) =>
      /^\w+(\(.+?\))?!:/.test(message) || /^BREAKING CHANGE:/m.test(message),
  );

  // Before 1.0, a breaking change bumps the minor version.
  if (breaking && major > 0) return `${major + 1}.0.0`;

  if (
    breaking ||
    subjects.some((subject) => /^feat(\(.+?\))?:/.test(subject))
  ) {
    return `${major}.${minor + 1}.0`;
  }

Install a plugin from a configured or remote marketplace.

Pass either `PLUGIN@MARKETPLACE` or pass `PLUGIN` with `--marketplace MARKETPLACE`.

Usage: codex plugin add [OPTIONS] <PLUGIN[@MARKETPLACE]>

Arguments:
  <PLUGIN[@MARKETPLACE]>
          Plugin selector to install: either PLUGIN@MARKETPLACE or PLUGIN with --marketplace

Options:
  -c, --config <key=value>
          Override a configuration value that would otherwise be loaded from `~/.codex/config.toml`.
          Use a dotted path (`foo.bar.baz`) to override nested values. The `value` portion is parsed
          as TOML. If it fails to parse as TOML, the raw string is used as a literal.
          
          Examples: - `-c model="o3"` - `-c 'sandbox_permissions=["disk-full-read-access"]'` - `-c
          shell_environment_policy.inherit=all`

          Marketplace name to use when PLUGIN does not include @MARKETPLACE

          Enable a feature (repeatable). Equivalent to `-c features.<name>=true`

Do not claim restarting Codex alone activates backend rebuilds if probe/code doesn't establish that. Also prefer querying installed state over broad || true error swallowing.

The Claude transcript is provider state, so copying the extension database alone
does not preserve it.

A worktree removed with **Remove worktree** is recreated on the next turn from
the task's branch, or from its base commit if the branch was deleted too.
Uncommitted changes discarded during removal do not return.

## Reconnect after a restart

Start the service with the same `SUBAGENT_EXTENSION_FOR_CODEX_DATA` value, then
check the task list. The data directory holds the database, worktrees and admin
token.

Disconnecting a client leaves the service and its tasks running. Stopping the
service interrupts its active turns. On restart:

- A turn that was running becomes interrupted.
- Steers that turn had not taken move to the front of its queue.
- A non-empty recovered queue pauses until you resume it or send another
  message.

If a submission or shutdown outcome is uncertain, check Chat and Activity before
sending again.

## Updates and service handoff

A plugin update installs the new version while the old version's service may
still run. The next stdio proxy to start compares itself with that service. It
reads `version`, `apiVersion` and `launcher` from `/health` and `installRoot`
from `service.json`. Versions compare by semver precedence, so a prerelease
such as `0.2.0-beta.1` is older than `0.2.0`.

| Running service                                                | The proxy                                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Same version, installation present                             | Uses it.                                                                        |
| Started by a stdio proxy, older or its installation removed    | Asks it to drain, then starts the new version once it exits.                    |
| Started by a stdio proxy, newer                                | Uses it if `apiVersion` matches. Otherwise asks you to update the plugin.       |
| Started another way (`npm run dev`, `npm start`, a supervisor) | Uses it if `apiVersion` matches. Otherwise refuses. It never stops the service. |

A draining service starts no new turns. It lets running turns finish for up to
10 minutes, then interrupts the rest as a restart does. Queued tasks stay
queued, and the new service starts them. Proxies keep using a draining service
that speaks the same API, and their next call after it exits starts the new
version. Proxies on another API wait for the new service.

Give development services their own `SUBAGENT_EXTENSION_FOR_CODEX_DATA` and `PORT`
so an installed plugin never finds them.

## Raise a task budget

Runtime and cost limits accumulate across turns. While the task is idle, use the
budget controls in Chat to raise a limit without sending a message. A
`send_message` call can also carry a `budget` update.

- Each limit can only increase. `null` removes it, and an unlimited limit cannot
  become finite.
- Applying a budget without a message needs at least one changed limit.
- Budget updates affect that task only. Settings changes apply to new tasks.
- Runtime includes time spent waiting for input.
- Cost is checked at response boundaries, so the response that crosses a limit
  can exceed it. Usage from interrupted turns may be missing.

## Preserve service state

1. Stop the service gracefully.
2. Back up the full data directory, including the SQLite files and worktrees.

Copying only a live SQLite database can miss its write-ahead log. Keep the
Claude runtime state on the machine that owns the worktrees. Moving it to
another machine does not ensure native session continuation.

[Database](database.md) covers migrations and
[restoring a pre-migration backup](database.md#restore-a-backup).

## Earlier development data

Tasks created before edit recording have no recorded diffs, so their Changes tab
may be empty or unavailable. If you no longer need that data, stop the service
and start with a fresh data directory, after saving any worktrees and history
you need.

See [Local development](development.md) for `.env`, startup conflicts and

### Service address

The plugin uses port 17317 by default. If another program holds it and no service
owns the data directory, the proxy chooses a free port. The service saves its
address as `origin` in `<data-directory>/service.json`, where proxies and console
users can find it.

Setting `PORT`, `SUBAGENT_EXTENSION_FOR_CODEX_ORIGIN` or
`SUBAGENT_EXTENSION_FOR_CODEX_URL` fixes the address and disables port recovery.
If it is taken, choose a free port or remove the override.

workers that edit files and run commands.

`<data-directory>/admin-token` when needed and keeps it across restarts. An
environment override replaces the file's token without writing to the file.

The installed plugin uses the same default data directory as every other way of
running the service. It avoids the `PLUGIN_DATA` directory Codex gives plugins
because Codex may delete that directory on uninstall, along with task history
and worktree records.

See [Local development](development.md) for `.env`, startup conflicts and
packaging.

### Service address

The plugin uses port 17317 by default. If another program holds it and no service
owns the data directory, the proxy chooses a free port. The service saves its
address as `origin` in `<data-directory>/service.json`, where proxies and console
users can find it.

Setting `PORT`, `SUBAGENT_EXTENSION_FOR_CODEX_ORIGIN` or
`SUBAGENT_EXTENSION_FOR_CODEX_URL` fixes the address and disables port recovery.
If it is taken, choose a free port or remove the override.

workers that edit files and run commands.

environment override replaces the file's token without writing to the file.

626	
627	`npm run release:assemble`, run after a build, writes `release/`, the package
628	the release publishes to npm. It holds the packed files, a manifest with no
629	scripts or dependencies, and an `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` that lists
630	the plugin with source `./`. The directory is both a Codex marketplace and the
631	plugin. Install it locally with:
632	
633	```sh
634	codex plugin marketplace add ./release
635	codex plugin add subagent-extension-for-codex@demo-user
636	```
637	
638	Adding the checkout itself (`codex plugin marketplace add ./`) adds `main`'s
639	marketplace, which installs the version it lists from npm, so test local builds
640	with `./release`.
